items.title: George Wein interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001
items.q: a lot of the older critics were a little upset with me until I wrote them a letter, Dan Morgenstern and Ira Gitler, I wrote them a detailed letter

ctx.x: I won’t be on a panel. You’ll never get me sitting on a panel. Because I don’t like panels. You know, you want me to talk, if I can teach you something, if I can help you, or you can teach me something, great. Sitting on a panel — I was asked to be on a panel just recently and it was an interesting panel, but I said I had made a pact myself. I nearly weakened. And I had made a pact with myself. I wrote them a very nice note. I said, “I can’t break the pact I made with myself, I won’t sit on panels.” Last year I…

now carrying the ball all over the country in universities. Many of these people are here right now. And it was fascinating. And we’ll do that again. If we won’t do it this year, we’ll certainly do it next year. But it created a different kind of thing than the panel’s discussion where you have four people and somebody talks for five minutes and then somebody says something and somebody says well I don’t agree with that. I’m not interested whether you agree with it. Agree with it before or after the fact. And…

items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: So we hooked up with George Wein who then was running Storyville.

ctx.x: I had no thoughts at that time of becoming in any way professionally involved in the music, but I was — it was like 52nd Street was in its final stages, but it was still alive and it was no small thing to have Sidney Bechet at Jimmy Ryan’s and across the street maybe Charlie Parker if you were lucky and he was in town. And, you know, Billie Holiday at the Onyx Club. So there was still a lot going on. And this was, you know, still a vibrant time. There was downtown on weekends, there was the Stuyvesant Casino in…

not much more than a glorified messenger but I got to meet a lot of people and actually was talked into running for office at the American Newspaper Guild, a pretty left wing thing. I was a Wallace — Henry Wallace was running for president. That was that famous election when Truman — Truman and Dewey. And it was a great experience because I was working at Time Inc. I was at a nerve center there on election night, which was a studio where they were broadcasting, and there was a guy named H.V. Kaltenborn, who was —…

downstairs called Mahogany Hall, which was the traditional club, and upstairs was Storyville, and on Sunday afternoons both bands would play. And then at the end there would be some get-together. So the most remarkable thing that involved that kind of a Sunday afternoon was when Art Tatum’s trio was upstairs and Sidney Bechet was downstairs. And for the jam they got together and played as Sidney sat in with the Tatum trio, and they played “Lady Be Good” and that was a [gestures]. This was on the occasion — that…

items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I intersected with George too. It was George who made it possible for us to bring Art Tatum to Brandeis, and of course I had a long association with Festival Productions

ctx.x: . . . pantheon, which has, until about five years ago, only consisted of musicians. But they decided to add a category called “jazz advocate,” which is named for A. B. Spellman, who just retired about a year ago from his 30 years at NEA in the jazz program there. My predecessors were, first, Nat Hentoff, who after all is an old mentor of mine. Then it was George Wein, who we don’t need to say – everybody knows who George was. I intersected with George too. It was George who made it possible for us to bring Art…
Thank you for being present for the easiest interview I’ve ever had to conduct.

items.title: George Wein — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Dan is a little younger than I am and I don't know what he was doing, but he remembers that day of Bechet and Tatum.

ctx.x: He was a young kid and he was there. Dan is a little younger than I am and I don't know what he was doing, but he remembers that day of Bechet and Tatum. The other thing that we did, we brought up the band from downstairs and Charlie Parker was upstairs and I had Vic Dickenson and Doc Cheatham in the band, and I was playing piano, and I had Bird play with us.
